description: Hire Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2026.

talks.title: Wednesday
talks.teaser: Offers career-entry guidance for newcomers to security, from first roles and SOC paths to non-traditional backgrounds.
talks.summary:
This block from the Hire Ground stage opens with a session aimed at people starting out in security. The presenters argue that a first job is a stepping stone, that demonstrable skills and written-up lab work count for more than certifications alone, and that soft skills and networking carry real weight. They recommend inexpensive home labs built from retired hardware, keeping detailed notes that include failed attempts, and framing technical work in terms of business impact.

The next session covers security operations center careers, from tier-one analyst through senior and lead roles. The speakers discuss which certifications to pursue, favoring ones that match the tools a current employer uses, and keeping a running record of achievements to support performance reviews. They also describe how AI is changing triage work and why analysts still need to check its output. Later talks cover a move into security from medicine and military service, with advice on tailoring resumes to postings and joining local community groups, and a path from software testing into technical audit at a large company.

The throughline across the block is that newcomers should begin where they are, ask specific questions, practice explaining their work to non-technical people, and pace themselves to avoid burnout. The closing question-and-answer segment covered resume framing, approaching professionals for mentorship, and handling imposter feelings in interviews.

talks.title: Tuesday
talks.teaser: Covers certifications, hiring pitfalls, AI-era career advice and non-linear career paths across several Higher Ground talks.
talks.summary:
This stream from the Tuesday of BSides Las Vegas 2026 Higher Ground track bundles several career-focused talks. Michael R. Brown opens with a primer on security certifications: how they differ from certificates of completion, why they expire and require continuing education, and how the major certifying bodies and niche groups compare. He suggests starting with a generalist credential and then adding specialty certifications tied to a chosen path.

Carter Miller then treats hiring as a verification problem. He describes inflated résumés, candidates getting live help during interviews, proxy workers, fake applicants and keyword-based screening. His advice is to attach public proof of work to claims, probe depth with follow-up questions, and make sure each interview stage checks something specific.

Gmark and Michael discuss how AI is changing security jobs. Routine, checklist-style work looks most exposed, while accountability, judgment under uncertainty, leadership and interpersonal trust are harder to automate. Their practical guidance is to build small projects with AI tools, learn continuously, make your work visible and understand the business side. Jenna closes with a talk on non-linear careers, urging listeners to follow their energy, reflect on each role, build reputation and calibrate their instincts.

talks.title: Monday
talks.teaser: Covers security career paths, team building, CISO advice, job market trends and hiring tips across several sessions.
talks.summary:
This is a full day of career-focused sessions from the Hire Ground stage at a Las Vegas security conference, recorded as one stream. The opening session treats digital forensics as a career. A workplace scenario shows how event logs can hide what happened, and the speaker introduces the idea that every contact leaves a trace. The talk covers the difference between disk-based and live acquisition, chain of custody, how forensics relates to incident response, training routes, and the personal traits that suit the work. The speaker stresses that the job is slow and methodical.

The middle of the stream moves to leadership and hiring. One speaker shares a management philosophy and advice on building a talent pipeline, onboarding, retention, communication and basic project management. A panel of CISOs then answers audience questions on moving into leadership, being visible at work, mentoring, and handling self-doubt. A recruiter presents job-market data on where investment is flowing and which problem areas are likely to hire, and advises positioning skills around concrete problems solved.

The later sessions focus on getting hired. Speakers discuss resume tailoring, interview preparation, networking, and spotting job scams. A closing session groups security work into role families and suggests public GitHub projects and policy writing as proof of practical ability. The main takeaway is to choose a specific role family, build visible evidence of work, and stay connected to the community.
